s01.slug: TUESDAY · 3:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, UNDER THE OVERHANG
body: The alarm comes into the dream as a goose, and then it’s the goose-horn in the ceiling of 412 and the strobe going white on the crucifix, and it’s three in the morning. Theo is already at the door in the navy silk robe with a golf umbrella under his arm and both bags off the top shelf of the closet, the gray and the black. Jack gets the Carhartt off the hook and his feet into his shoes without socks and follows him down four flights of people swearing.

Outside, the storm has come in the dark. Not rain yet, mostly: wind, straight off the Lagoon and hard enough to lean on, and the eucalyptus behind Anacapa thrashing over the roofline with the sound of surf in the wrong place, the menthol smell of them torn open and blowing everywhere. A branch the size of a canoe lies across the bike path. Then the rain, sideways, a bucketful at a time, out of a sky Jack can’t see.

Three hundred and ten people cannot stand on the Delgado lawn tonight, so they don’t. They jam in under the concrete overhang along the front of the building and under the carport of the Anacapa lot, in boxers and towels and comforters and a collective mood. Somebody has brought a pillow. Somebody has brought a girl from another dorm, and both of them would prefer that not be discussed.
Priya is out in the fire lane with the air horn in one hand and the other hand held high over her head, and in it, sealed in a gallon Ziploc against the weather, a laminate.

body: Kevin is calling the roll off a clipboard he keeps zipped inside his quarter-zip between names. “If you can hear me, you’re alive,” he tells the fourth floor, “and if you’re alive, you’re accounted for. That’s just science.”

Margot is dry. There is no account for this. She stands at the dead center of the overhang in a black raincoat buttoned to the throat with the Moleskine open on her palm, and the rain, which has gotten everybody else, appears to have declined her. She checks her watch against the page. “Twenty-five,” she tells Jack. Eighteen days from the last one would have been last Tuesday, and last Tuesday the building slept like a baby. She looks out at the storm with professional disappointment. “Either he’s irregular,” she says, “or he’s two people.” She puts the Moleskine away in an inside pocket, where it stays dry too.

At the far end of the building the wrong fire door swings open and Doug Pruitt comes out of it into the weather, barefoot, his pillow under his arm, and walks straight through the ankle-deep puddle at the bottom of the steps and fetches up under the overhang.

Theo holds the golf umbrella over himself, the two bags and Laney, in that order of priority. Laney is wearing a Hefty bag. It’s a black contractor bag with a hole torn in it for her face, and she has put her pearls on over it.

And Lena is at the other end of the overhang. Alone, at the very edge, where the rain gets her every time it comes and she doesn’t move in out of it. She’s in a man’s green Tulane sweatshirt that can only be Wes’s, left behind or left on purpose: the hood up, the sleeves pulled down over her hands, the green gone soft and pale with washing and TULANE across the chest in a white that is mostly memory. The hem comes to mid-thigh, over sleep shorts, over the Justins, unlaced. Thirty dry people separate her from Laney, and the two of them are not speaking, and thirty people in comforters are carefully standing in it. Jack doesn’t know why, and no one’s said.

The last time he saw her was Monday morning in the Anacapa lot, with Wes’s duffel going into the back of the Odyssey. The last time he heard her was Monday night, two floors down the stairwell, on the phone, and he has had the sound of it in his ear since. She sees him. She pushes the hood back with the back of her wrist.
“Morning, Jack.”
Polite. The weekend is in it.

journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log. Tuesday the 6th, nothing. Either the theory’s wrong or he’s on vacation. Alarm 3, Tuesday the 13th, 3:20, in a storm, under the overhang: twenty-five days. Margot says he’s irregular or he’s two people.

response: He goes down the overhang through thirty people and stands at the edge with her, where the rain gets him too. She lets him. She says nothing, and he says nothing back, and the rain has plenty to say on its own. When the all-clear goes at 3:41 she says, “Thank you,” to the lawn, and goes in first.

In the fourth-floor hall Laney falls in behind Theo and Jack with her pillow. “I’ve been *exiled*. From my own *room*. s02.slug: TUESDAY · 3:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY MAILBOXES
body: No mail Monday, for Columbus, so Tuesday there are two days of it, and at ten to four the Delgado lobby smells like wet wool and wet cardboard and two hundred people’s rain. What the alarm was announcing has arrived in full. It comes down the lobby glass in sheets so thick the fire lane is a rumor, and the palms out front are bent double. The day attendant at the front desk is reading a *Cosmo* somebody left in the lounge and doesn’t look up for anybody.

*The Moviegoer* is in Jack’s back pocket, the Vintage paperback with its spine cracked white, out of the milk crate this morning because Binx Bolling is on a search and Jack has a paper due tomorrow at one about whether a man can know his own heart, and so far the paper is a title. Hale’s Williams is upstairs on the desk, where it has been reminding him all week of the margins he owes it.

His box has a Newman flyer, a credit card offer for JOHN COSTIGAN, and the envelope: block capitals, DANIEL F. COSTIGAN and the number after it, the return address printed by the institution, a Leavittsburg postmark from Friday. He opens it standing at the mailboxes.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
PROFESSOR,
The Hopkins came. Took me a week to get past the first one but then I got to Felix Randal, the horse guy, the blacksmith, and I read it to Ma on the phone Tuesday and she cried, so thanks for that, I’m telling you so you know I read it. Not so you feel bad.
The Housman came too. Tell your man who don’t sleep that nobody in here does either. Number LIV made Reggie cry and Reggie is from Portsmouth.
Ma says there’s a girl now. Becca. From Idaho. Ma says she’s a nice girl. Ma says it how she says the Browns got a nice stadium.
Did you tell Lena hey or do I got to come out there.
Reggie asked me do I ever wish I did it different. I told him I don’t wish. I decided. It’s different.
Push-ups 140. Browns are 0-4 so don’t call me about it.
—D.

body: Jack stands at the mailboxes with the letter open in his hands. Behind him the door lets in a gust and a girl with a broken umbrella, and the umbrella goes into the trash can by the desk with a sound like a bird hitting a window, and the attendant turns a page. The rain keeps coming down the glass. Jack stands there until the girl is gone and the lobby is just the rain again.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140.

body: The harbor is having the worst night of its year. The boats in the slips knock against the pilings without letup, the sea lions who bark under the docks every other night of the week have gone dead quiet, and the rain comes across the wharf in sheets and drums on the glass of the window booth, which is empty. They’re all empty. Tuesday is half-price chowder, and tonight it is half-price chowder for no one. Ray Ochoa’s stool, where the meatloaf goes on Tuesdays, is bare. Jack has run the Hobart three times since seven mostly to have something to do with his hands, and his share of the tip jar is shaping up to be a dime and a peppermint.

At a quarter past nine Gloria comes out from behind the register with the pencil through her gray bun and a quarter in her fingers, walks the length of the empty room to the jukebox, puts the quarter in, and plays Sinatra into a gale. She doesn’t explain it. She walks back to the register. On the shelf over the pass Rudy’s transistor has KCBX instead of the Dodgers, a man reading out wind speeds and running low on synonyms for *heavy*.

The only customers since eight are two women at the counter in Harbor Inn housekeeping smocks under their rain jackets, one in her fifties and one maybe twenty-five, waiting out a 7 bus that was supposed to come at eight, then at ten. Gloria has put soup and grilled cheese in front of them and written no ticket, and when the older one went for her purse Gloria looked at her until she stopped. The younger one is showing the older one pictures on a phone with a cracked face, a baby in a pumpkin hat, and the older one is unimpressed on principle.
Gloria fills their cups. “Dulce. Rosario. This one’s Jack. He knows your New Orleans girl.”

Jack, at the end of the counter with a bus tub on his hip, knows one New Orleans girl, and can’t think how she could be theirs. Rosario looks him over, apron to cowlick, and says something to Dulce in Spanish, quick, and Dulce laughs into her soup.

From the pass, without looking up from the flattop, Rudy translates. “They say your friend brings soup. Sundays. To the hotel, for the night shift.” Dulce adds something, pointing her spoon at Jack. “The New Orleans girl,” Rudy says. Dulce adds one more thing, and Rosario nods hard, agreeing. Rudy scrapes the grill. “They say it needs salt.”
Jack didn’t know. He thought he knew a fair amount about where Lena Broussard is on a given night of the week, and he didn’t know that.
At the end of the counter Gloria comes back with the pot and fills his coffee, which he did not ask for, and stands there with it.

body.text: “Saturday,” she says. “Merle. You got a laugh.”
“Saturday,” she says. “Merle. You said it to his face.” She holds the pot. “Pie or the door, hon. I heard you.”
“Saturday,” she says. “That fisherman. You kept your mouth shut.” She holds the pot. “Pie or the door, hon.”

s04.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY
body: The walk from the bus stop on Ocean Road was four hundred yards of horizontal water, and Jack’s one clean pair of jeans is soaked through, so at twenty to two in the morning he goes down to the basement in gym shorts with the jeans in a wet wad under his arm to put them in a dryer and stand in front of it.

The laundry room is warm and smells the way it always smells, sweet and chemical, dryer sheets and lint and somebody’s abandoned towels going sour in a washer. Eight washers. Six dryers, three of them dark tonight and three tumbling. Against the far wall, the old upright piano with its lid down, the one with the dead F that nobody in Delgado admits to playing.

Priya is sitting on the floor by the door at the back marked RA STORAGE — NOT A STUDY ROOM, in Facilities stencil, black. She has the hood of her Fremont High sweatshirt up and a Ziploc of orgo flashcards on her knees, and she has packed every towel in the laundry room along the bottom of the door in a dam, including several that are not hers. Water is coming under it anyway. A dark tongue of it has gotten past the towels and is spreading across the linoleum toward the dryers.
“The laundry room closes at eleven,” she says, without looking up.
“You’re here.”

“I’m *staff*.” She turns a flashcard over, reads it, turns it back. “I have orgo at eight a.m. It’s warm down here, the dryers, 401 is a refrigerator. I have my library shift tomorrow night, midnight to eight. And I have a *lake* in my *closet*.”

She stands up with a ring of keys, forty of them, color-coded with nail polish, and finds the purple one on the third try. The door opens inward on two inches of storm water, brown, come in through the window well and lying flat and still over the whole floor of the closet. Holiday decorations in a box marked DECEMBER. A carton of confiscated candles, labeled. Last year’s lost-and-found in a black garbage bag slumped against the wall. And on the floor at the back, in the water, a banker’s box with a Sharpie label: CALLOWAY · 222 · HOLD FOR FAMILY. HOLD is underlined twice. The bottom corner of the box has gone dark and soft.
Jack knows the name. Priya told it to him over a grocery cupcake at about this hour of a Wednesday, five weeks ago.

They lift it out together, careful of the soft corner, and set it on top of a working dryer, which is warm. Priya opens the lid to check the damage. A gray sweatshirt that says SELMA HIGH. CDs in a zip case. A mug. A photo of two girls laughing in a dorm window with the blinds pulled up crooked, and one of them is Priya, with bangs. A black-and-white composition book, the bottom edge of it wet and ruffling. Priya picks that up last and opens the cover. Only the cover.

body.title: Inside the cover
body.text: Nora Calloway · Delgado 222 · If found, please return. Reward: I’ll sing you something.

body: She closes it. “I’ve never gotten past this page.” She sets it back on top of the sweatshirt and squares it with the edge of the box, twice. Serra sent it over in May, because 222 was the address on the paperwork, and Priya signed for it. The Calloways never came for it. She can’t throw it out, and she can’t mail it. “You can’t mail somebody their daughter’s *mug*.”

Then she breaks, completely and at speed. “I *tutor* organic chemistry. I’m *failing* organic chemistry. My parents think I’m going to be a doctor. They run a *motel*.” She sits down on the dryer beside the box with her flashcards in her lap and cries hard, for about forty seconds, with her mouth open, and the dryer goes on tumbling under her.

Laney is asleep on the Aerobed in Theo’s navy silk, flat on her back with her hands folded on her stomach, snoring delicately through her nose, a lady about it even unconscious. Theo is at his desk in the dark with his headphones on and the MacBook lit, some French film going in black and white with the subtitles crawling, and he isn’t watching it.
Jack sits up on his bed with the yellow legal pad on his knee. At the top of it, underlined, in his own hand since Monday night: *That a Man Can Know His Own Heart.* Under that, two days of nothing.

body: He writes the first sentence.
*A man knows his own heart by what he says yes to.*

Then the rest comes, faster than his hand. Aristotle, *Ethics* II: we become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave ones, and the knowing comes after the doing, not before. James 2:18, *I by my works will show you my faith.* Binx Bolling on his search, who can’t find himself by looking and finds out who he is by what he does on a Wednesday. And Augustine, who is supposed to be her side of this: for a man who said he couldn’t know his own heart, he filled ten books with it. Jack fills two pages of the pad and turns it over and keeps going. He has Percy open on the blanket, spine up, and the pen going, and across the room the French film plays on in Theo’s headphones, small and tinny, and the rain keeps on at the window, and so does the pen.

Two hours of sleep and a shower that ran hot for ninety seconds. When Jack comes back into 412 with his towel around his neck, the room has become another country. Laney’s monogrammed laptop is propped against Theo’s mirror at full volume, Jay Sean’s falsetto and then Lil Wayne under it, loud enough to go through two floors.
“It’s for 217,” Laney says, by way of good morning. Two floors down. “A diplomatic gesture. Lil Wayne is a *New Orleans* boy. It’s an olive branch with a *beat*.”

She isn’t at the mirror. She’s at Theo’s desk in Theo’s navy silk robe, her hair up in one of his towels, and Theo is beside her in the black Meridian one, their heads together over a yellow legal pad. Theo turns the pad face down with one finger. He doesn’t hurry; Theo never hurries anything he can do beautifully instead. Jack reads it upside down before it goes over: HALLOWEEN, and under it, underlined twice, SEATING.
“Are you two —”
“No.” Both of them, at once, in harmony.
Laney floats back to the mirror. On the laptop, behind the music, her Facebook is open to her own wall.

body: She starts on her face: a sponge, a little bottle, the freckles going under one patch of cheek at a time.

Kevin appears in the doorway with his orgo cards rubber-banded in four colors and a shaker bottle of something the color of wet cement. He takes in the Aerobed, the navy silk, a second toothbrush standing in Theo’s Harvard-Westlake mug. “This,” Kevin says, “is a fire code violation and a cry for help.”
“I’m a *refugee*, Kevin.”

The radiator knocks twice, the way it does. Midterm week: half the table hasn’t slept. Caleb’s *Consolations* is shedding Post-its onto the oak faster than usual. Yusuf has a steel thermos of tea and has drawn a small bridge in his margin, with arrows.
Hale is in his chair before any of them again — the second time this term — with the roster squared in front of him and his hands folded on top of it.

Lena comes in at a minute to one. A dark skirt and the Justins, the green sweatshirt under the oatmeal cardigan, its cuffs hanging out past the cardigan’s. She takes the chair across from Jack, which is hers, and squares her paper to the edge of the table, and looks at him for the first time since the overhang.
“Good afternoon, Mr. Costigan.”
He has been Mr. Costigan before, for three days in September. He thought they were done with it.
Hale’s head comes up from the roster. “Mr. Costigan has been demoted,” he says, to the table at large. “How interesting.”

Then the titles. “‘That a Man Can Know His Own Heart.’ Mr. Costigan. ‘That He Cannot.’ Miss Broussard.” He reads the text off a single sheet without needing to look down much. “Jeremiah, seventeen. *The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately corrupt; who can understand it? I the Lord search the mind and try the heart.*” He sets the sheet down. “Note who’s speaking. The only one in the text who claims to know it is the one I don’t believe in. Mr. Costigan, you have been asked to steal His job. Miss Broussard has merely been asked to agree with Him, which for a Catholic is a dull afternoon.”

“Al-Anfal,” Yusuf says, precise, not looking up from his bridge. “Eight twenty-four. *Know that God comes between a man and his heart.*” He caps his pen. “Which means no one else gets in there either.”
“Selah,” says Caleb.

“No blood today,” Hale says. “It’s midterm week and I am not a monster, only a professor. You will swap, you will bleed on each other by Monday, and I’ll have the corpses at one. Thursday you have my midterm, which will be worse.”
The papers cross the oak. Hers comes to him squared; his goes to her the same way, and she’s reading his before it stops moving.
“In the meantime,” Hale says, and leans back. “Mr. Costigan. The Almighty’s job. Tell us how you mean to pull off the burglary.”

Theo has brought his own Martinelli’s. He fills a plastic cup with it, stands, and raises it to the room. “To capitalism. It came back.”
“Tell Lordstown,” Jack says.
His father has been laid off since June. Ohio is pushing ten percent. Whatever came back today hasn’t been told the way to the garage on Glenwood Avenue.
Theo considers this, without irony. “I’ll tell my father,” he says. “He’ll want to option it.”

Laney, in exile at Theo’s table, is eating a waffle with a knife and fork, in small square pieces, with the posture of a girl being judged on it. She has not looked two tables over once, and the effort shows in her neck.

Two tables over, Lena and Margot are sharing a plate of the waffle iron’s bad waffles. Lena is talking with her hands, a fork in one of them, building something in the air over the syrup; Margot is listening with her chin on her fist. Then Margot’s eyes come up and catch Jack looking. Margot looks down at her plate.

s09.slug: WEDNESDAY · 9:05 PM · PACIFICA LIBRARY, EIGHTH FLOOR
body: For midterm week the Brick doesn’t close; a sign on an easel in the lobby says so, OPEN 24 HOURS, with a clip-art owl. The eighth floor is the silent floor. Long tables run along the windows, and the windows are black with the post-storm dark, so that the Channel Islands are out there somewhere and might as well not be. At the far end a grad student is asleep under his own coat with one sock showing. Kevin has a table against the stacks, his cards squared by color.

Lena has the window table at the very end: *The Habit of Being*, a steel thermos, a red pen, and Jack’s paper. Jack has a table in the middle of the floor with *The Moviegoer*, the Williams, a red pen and her paper. He is wearing Danny’s Carhartt because the building hasn’t caught up with the weather. Twenty yards of carpet. They haven’t said a word to each other since he came up at eight. Every so often, down at the end, a cap comes off a pen.

Wet coats are drying on the backs of chairs. The fluorescent tubes hum a note just under hearing, the kind you only notice when it stops. He has her paper open to Aquinas and nothing written beside it yet. He tries Binx instead: *The search is what anyone would undertake if he were not sunk in the everydayness of his own life.* He underlines it, which he did once already in Youngstown in pencil, and now there are two lines under it, gray and red.

At the far end Lena pushes the sleeves of the green sweatshirt up to her elbows, both of them, and bends to his second page with the red pen. He knows what the sleeves mean. He has lost arguments to them since August.

body: By midnight the eighth floor is two lamps and a sleeping grad student. Two people at two tables, marking each other’s arguments in red. The clementine is still on her table by the thermos, unpeeled. His is in the Ziploc with the earplugs. Out past the black glass a few stars have come through where the storm tore the clouds open.

At a quarter past twelve Kevin snaps a last rubber band around a last stack and gets up, and on his way past Jack’s table he stops. He looks down the carpet at the far lamp, and back at Jack, and the big easy smile doesn’t move at all. “Sleep is a study strategy,” he says. “So is a different floor.” Then the big easy smile, and he goes down the stairs.

At twenty past, Jack is at her last line. *A woman who says she knows her own heart is either a saint or lying.* He uncaps the red pen and writes beside it, before he can decide not to: *Which are you?*
He caps the pen and goes back to Aquinas.

At twelve thirty-five he needs air. The elevator takes him down eight floors. At the overnight circulation desk Priya is on her shift in the Fremont High hoodie, shuffling a Ziploc of orgo flashcards for a midterm she took at eight yesterday morning, on her birthday. body: Four in the morning is the hour nobody built the Brick for. The heat gave up around two. Every table on the eighth floor is empty but his, hers, and the grad student’s at the far end, where the coat has risen and fallen on the same slow breath since midnight. The storm took the clouds with it. Out past the glass there are stars over the water and no moon, so the windows give back only the room: two lamps, a guy in a Carhartt with a red pen, and down at the end a girl in Wes’s sweatshirt who hasn’t looked up since one.

Then she does. She caps her pen, picks his paper up off her table and comes up the carpet with it, and puts it down in front of him open past the title page. Beside his first sentence — *A man knows his own heart by what he says yes to* — in red, in capitals, hard enough to dent the page:

body.text: THEN WHAT DID YOU TELL HIM?

body: He slides hers back across the table. She goes to the last page without looking for it, and there is his red beside her last line: *Which are you?* She reads it standing. She doesn’t sit.

She bends to say it, because it’s a silent floor and she was raised right. “First Corinthians four. *I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted.*” Her finger comes down on his sentence, on the word *yes*. “The man who wrote half the New Testament wouldn’t take his own heart’s word for it. And you’d take yours.” He can smell the chicory from her thermos on her. “You’d take yours on a *beach*.”

body.text: “You win, Mr. Costigan,” Lena says. Cold, not loud. “Write it down.” She goes back through the door to the eighth floor ahead of him, and the door swings shut in his face, and he stands on the landing with the EXIT sign and what he won.

“You still forfeit,” Lena says. She looks down the well, at eight floors of green rail going around into the dark, and when she says the rest it’s very quiet. “Seacliff’s mine.” He doesn’t ask. She holds the door for him. Only the door.
“Then what am I?”

The EXIT sign hums. She looks at him, and he doesn’t look away. The question goes down the shaft, eight floors of concrete, and none of it comes back up. They stand on the landing with it. Then, very carefully: “I have a midterm at nine-thirty.” “Same one,” Jack says.
She’s quiet a moment. Then: “Then we’re both lying, some days.” She watches to see if he catches it. He does. Then, very carefully: “I have a midterm at nine-thirty.” “Same one,” Jack says.
“Fine,” Lena says. “Your paper wins.” She lets that stand on the landing long enough to hurt. Then, formal, not cold: “It’s still wrong.”

The fire door opens. The grad student from the far end stands in it in his coat, hair flat on one side, the seam of a table printed down his cheek. “Some of us,” he says, “are failing quals.” The door swings shut on him. They’re laughing before it’s latched, out loud, both of them, helplessly, at four in the morning on a fire stair.
“A man can’t know his own heart,” Lena says. She’s above him on the stairs, and she looks down at him and lets him look back. “Exhibit A.”

The louvers overhead are open to the weather, and the wind comes straight down through them. A bench worn pale. In front of it a keyboard like a giant’s piano: two rows of oak batons, rounded by forty years of hands, and under them a pedalboard of longer keys for the feet. Below them, the tower door. A voice. Then a flashlight beam coming up the shaft, slowly, flight by flight, stopping at each window slit to have a look out.

Lena is crouched against the wall with her knees up and her breath going white. Jack has his hand flat on the cold bronze beside her head to keep his balance and doesn’t move it. She’s in Wes’s sweatshirt and, over it, the Carhartt.

The beam comes up into the cabin under them. Through the gaps in the frame he watches it go over the batons, the bench, the laminated sign, and hold there, while a radio on somebody’s shoulder crackles to itself.
“Nobody’s dumb enough,” the cop tells the radio, and goes back down.

They stay crouched until the cruiser’s engine starts on the lawn, and until it backs off the grass, and until its taillights have gone out of the Commons. Jack has to put his forehead against the bronze to keep from laughing. Lena doesn’t laugh at all. She glares at him over the corduroy collar, fierce and wet-eyed, one finger up — *don’t you dare* — and keeping still under that look is harder than keeping still for the cop was.

body: At five o’clock in the morning, two days after the first storm of the fall, Lena brings her fists down on the oak, and the Ferrer Tower plays “When the Saints Go Marching In” to the sleeping campus.

Badly. Magnificently. The bells come down through the louvers and the glass and the soles of his shoes, so loud up here it’s less a sound than a weather, bronze going off over their heads in the dark. She plays with her fists, both of them, loosely closed, forearms and all — and the first time she reaches for the bass he understands that that’s how the thing is meant to be played. Either she knew or she guessed. Either way the bells agree with her.

From the hatch he hears it come down the tower around him. The steel rail under his hand hums with every note, up from his palm and into his teeth.
She came in on the *and*. He’s still counting, out loud, uselessly, under it, and grinning like an idiot.

Across the Commons the lights start coming on. Delgado first, then Cabrillo, then Portolá, window after window, the dark grid of Anacapa filling in square by square like somebody doing the crossword in pen. From a fourth-floor window in Delgado somebody hollers it back across the lawn — WHO DAT — and is never identified. On the oak beside the batons the RAZR buzzes in a little circle.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t.

“You didn’t move,” Lena says. “No.” “Your arm’s dead, isn’t it.” “Since six.” Six. Seven. He’s the one who sits back.
She shrugs out of the Carhartt and lays it over the chair beside him, and gathers up the peel, her paper, the thermos, *The Habit of Being*.

body: Sandoval Hall 1 at half past nine on a midterm morning smells like four hundred people who didn’t sleep: burnt coffee, Red Bull, wet hair, floor wax the storm tracked back up the aisles. Orange flip-down seats, row on row; blue books going down the rows hand to hand.

Row M. Margot on the inside, all in black, three sharpened pencils laid side by side on the fold-down desk in order of length. Lena in the aisle seat. She has showered; her hair is still wet, combed back with her fingers, darkening the shoulders of the green sweatshirt. The tote is at her feet with the mantilla folded on top of everything, black lace, ready for the 12:10. Jack sits in Row P, as instructed.

body.text: She hasn’t turned her head once since she sat down.

body: Hale is at the lectern with his hair wet too and wine on the cuff of the linen jacket, holding the wireless microphone in one hand as if somebody has asked him to dispose of it.

“Somebody played a gospel number on the Ferrer carillon at five o’clock this morning,” he says. “Badly. I was awake; I’m always awake. In eleven years it is the first thing that tower has done that I’ve enjoyed.” He surveys the room and nobody in it in particular. “One bell is still flat. You have seventy-five minutes. Begin.”
Four hundred blue books open. In Row M, Margot turns her head and looks at Lena, and keeps looking at her. Lena writes her name.

body.title: PHIL 1 · Midterm · Essay (40 points)
body.text: Aquinas’s First Way. State it; then break it.

body: Jack writes *The argument from motion* across the top of the first page, and under it the shape he could draw in his sleep. Some things in the world are in motion. Whatever is moved is moved by another. It can’t go back forever, or nothing would be moving now. So there is a first mover, moved by nothing, and this everyone understands to be God. He has written it a dozen times. He explained it on the home bleachers at Mariner Field at halftime, with Miley Cyrus coming out of the PA, to a girl in a Carhartt vest who said it back to him perfectly, and —

The pen stops. *Aquinas and football. That’s the dream girl right there.* He said it on the eighth floor of the Brick before it was light, and he didn’t hear it. He hears it now. A girl who can give you the *Summa* by question and article without looking anything up. A girl who made the owner of Sully’s surrender the bell over his own bar. He described Lena Broussard to Lena Broussard, on a library floor, at six in the morning, with half of her clementine in his hand.
He looks down to Row M. She’s writing fast, left hand flat on the blue book, head down, the wet hair over one shoulder. Her pen doesn’t stop.

choices.text: State it and defend it. Write it like it’s true.
response: It is true, so he writes it that way: the motion, the mover, the chain that can’t hang from nothing. Six pages in a borrowed confidence that feels, for six pages, like his own.
At 10:45 Hale says “Pens down,” and the blue books go hand over hand down the rows to the aisles, and his goes with them.

choices.text: Break it honestly — Hume, the regress, all of it.
response: He gives the objection everything it has — why not a chain with no first link, why not the universe as its own mover — and then answers it, and the answer is thinner than the objection, and he says so. In ink. To an atheist.
At 10:45 Hale says “Pens down,” and the blue books go hand over hand down the rows to the aisles, and his goes with them.

choices.text: Write the First Way and nothing else, fast. Don’t look down Row M again.
response: He doesn’t look. He writes it clean in twenty minutes and sits for forty more with his hands flat on the desk, studying the graffiti carved into the seat back in front of him. Somebody named DEREK has been here since 1994. He reads it forty minutes’ worth.
At 10:45 Hale says “Pens down,” and the blue books go hand over hand down the rows to the aisles, and his goes with them.

body: The whole lecture comes out onto the Sandoval steps into a washed, glittering sun, the storm gone east over the hills and the sky above the Commons scrubbed a blue so new it looks wet. Everyone is comparing answers. Everyone got the regress wrong. Down on the path Lena is already going, the tote on her shoulder and the green sweatshirt bright against the grass, off toward Ocean Road and St. Brendan’s.
The RAZR goes twice in his pocket.

body: The memorial of St. Teresa of Ávila, and Osei in white. About twenty-five people are scattered under the upturned hull of the ceiling, and the noon sun comes through the blue glass and lays itself over the pews in pieces. The 12:10 is the Mass of people with a lab at one: grad students, two nurses in scrubs, a man in a Caltrans vest with his hard hat on the kneeler. Mrs. Fitch has the front pew on the shrine side, as she has every weekday since the Carter administration, and beside her, in the black mantilla, is Lena.

Becca slides in next to Jack during the first reading, out of breath, in the Carhartt vest, smelling of seawater and squid. She looks at him sideways and her whisper is pure alarm. “You look *exhausted*. Were you at the library all night?”

response: “Till seven.”
It’s true. Every word of it is true.

choices.text: “Till seven. Lena was there too. We fought about our papers.”
choices.key: At the 12:10 Becca asked if you were at the library all night. You told her Lena was there too.
response: “Till seven,” Jack says. “Lena was there too. We fought about our papers.”

“Oh, *good*,” Becca whispers, and means it all the way down. “I hate when people study alone.” She looks up the church at the black mantilla in the front pew, fond, and back at him. It would have been easier if she’d minded.

choices.key: At the 12:10 Becca asked if you were at the library all night. You said till two.
response: “Till two,” he says.
“Two!” Pure delight, whispered. “That’s when I pray.” She looks at him as if he’s handed her a present. He takes it.

body.text: She squeezes his hand on the pew. He read her text at 6:41 this morning on the eighth floor, with the phone in his shirt pocket and Lena asleep against his arm.
body.else: She squeezes his hand on the pew. “I prayed at two,” she whispers, as news. He knows. He read it at 6:41 this morning on the eighth floor, with the phone in his shirt pocket and Lena asleep against his arm.

body: Osei keeps the homily to three sentences, which is two more than he sometimes uses. Teresa was on the road to found a convent, the story goes, when her cart went over into a river and put her in it, habit and all, and climbing out soaked she told the Lord what she thought of Him. “‘If this is how You treat Your friends,’” Osei says, “‘no wonder You have so few.’” He folds his hands on the ambo. “She is a Doctor of the Church. She was also correct.”
In the front pew Lena laughs out loud, once, the sound bright and unembarrassed in the quiet church, and Mrs. Fitch turns to look at her, and if the look reaches Lena, it doesn’t show.

At Communion Jack goes up behind Becca and comes back and kneels, and for the length of the thanksgiving nothing in him is arguing with anything. He has had no sleep, and the blue book is still in his hand somewhere, and the bleachers, and the eighth floor; and for a minute or so none of it is in charge. He couldn’t tell anyone where that comes from.
After, on the steps in the sun, Lena comes out with Mrs. Fitch on her arm and the mantilla coming off in one pull. Becca goes straight to her. “Is Teresa the one with the angel? With the arrow?”

body.text: “That’s her.” Lena folds the lace into a square, then a smaller square. “First woman Doctor of the Church. Paul the Sixth, 1970. Catherine got hers a week later and has never gotten over it.”
body.else: “That’s her.” Lena folds the lace into a square, then a smaller square. “First woman Doctor of the Church. Paul the Sixth, 1970. Catherine had to wait a week.”

body: “I *love* that!” Becca says.

Jack stands on the step below the two of them, two nights’ sleep short, with the sun in his eyes. Lena’s eyes come to him and stay as long as manners allow, which in New Orleans is a precise amount of time, and then go back to Becca, and she says something kind about the vest. Then she takes Mrs. Fitch down the steps and off toward the parking lot, the folded lace showing at the top of the tote.
Becca puts her arm through his. She has an hour before the touch tank and she has a plan for them. “You’re eating,” she says. “Then I’m feeding a bat ray.”

s17b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL
body: The Fishbowl at twenty to twelve: every couch taken, the arms of every couch taken, people cross-legged on the carpet and two deep against the glass with their backpacks still on. On the TV bolted in the corner, CNN, and on CNN a silver balloon the shape of a Jiffy Pop lid, sliding across a brown Colorado sky in a long helicopter shot. A six-year-old boy may be inside, the banner says. The anchors have put on their serious voices and keep having to take them off to say the word *balloon*.

Laney is on the middle couch in Theo’s navy silk robe over jeans, the exile’s uniform, both feet tucked under her. She has been calling it since eleven. “And our next contestant,” she says, “is a *weather event*. She hails from Fort Collins. She enjoys altitude and long drifts on the jet stream, and her talent tonight is —”
“Picture it,” Theo says from the arm of the couch. “A boy. A balloon. A nation holding its breath. Ninety minutes, Dennis Quaid as the dad.”

Kevin is on the floor with his back against the couch and the orgo midterm still visible in his face. “Okay, so at seven thousand feet ambient’s maybe forty degrees, and if it climbs to ten, fifteen thousand, the partial pressure of oxygen drops off a cliff, and a kid that size, with that surface area —” He stops. It has stopped being a bit, and he’s the one who stopped it. He puts his chin on his knees.

Margot stands at the glass with her arms folded and her coat still buttoned. “That balloon,” she says, “is too calm to have a child in it.” A girl from the third floor shushes her. Margot accepts the shush without any change of expression and goes on watching the balloon with the expression she uses on footnotes. On the far couch Doug Pruitt wakes, looks at the screen, says “Huh,” and goes back to sleep.
Theo moves his feet off the coffee table so Jack can sit on it, and hands him half of a cold breakfast burrito in its foil, and asks him, pleasantly, what he thinks of the weather.

At 12:35 it comes down. A field northeast of Denver, the silver skin folding in on itself like a dropped umbrella, men running at it from a truck, and the little compartment under it empty. Then somebody on CNN says a deputy thinks he saw something fall, back near a town called Platteville. Laney stops calling it. She pulls a throw pillow into her stomach and holds it there, and the room goes quiet under the TV.

At ten to one Lena comes in from the 12:10. The mantilla is folded in the tote. She doesn’t sit; she stands behind the middle couch with the tote on her shoulder, and she doesn’t look at the empty balloon in the field. She’s reading the crawl under it.

body.title: The CNN crawl
body.text: OBAMA IN NEW ORLEANS · FIRST VISIT AS PRESIDENT · TOWN HALL AT UNIVERSITY OF NEW ORLEANS · STOPS AT LOWER NINTH WARD SCHOOL

body: Her city, and her president, on a strip of type under a field in Colorado. Jack sees what she’s reading. Her face doesn’t make a speech about it either way. On the couch, without turning around, Laney moves her bag off the cushion beside her. Lena stays where she is, standing, and the crawl comes around to New Orleans again, white letters going right to left under the men walking the field in a line.

s18.slug: THURSDAY · 2:15 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE FISHBOWL

body.text: Jack has been in the Fishbowl since twenty to two, when Becca squeezed his arm in the lobby and went down the bluff to the Marine Lab. He came in on an empty balloon in a field, a deputy who thinks he saw something fall, and Laney with a throw pillow held against her stomach.
Lena went upstairs to sleep a little after one, without a word to anybody. Laney watched her go in the reflection on the glass.

body: On CNN, deputies walk a field in a line with their heads down. Kevin is on his feet now, pacing behind the couch with his hands laced on top of his crew cut. Then the sheriff of Larimer County comes on at a podium in a parking lot. “And our *final* contestant,” Laney says, low, to nobody, “hails from Larimer County —” and stops, because the sheriff is talking, and the Fishbowl holds still: the boy is at home. He’s fine. He was found hiding in a cardboard box in the attic above the garage.

The room comes apart. A cheer goes up loud enough to bring the desk attendant out from behind the front desk, somebody hugs a stranger, Doug sits up for it. Laney cries a little and points at her own face. “This is the *mascara*. It’s defective. I’m writing to Lancôme.” Kevin sits down on the carpet, hard, and laughs at the ceiling.
Jack doesn’t cheer. Pauger Street, he thinks, and an axe coming back off the cypress. He sits on the coffee table with his hands between his knees while the Fishbowl cheers a boy in a box.

Then the day takes him. Evan lets the four o’clock section out of Hollis 108 at twenty past, because nobody in it has a voice left. La Flaca comes out of its chain behind Delgado with the seat still wet. The Anchor, seven to one, every stool taken, the Thursday crowd back after the storm, the Hobart, the steam, Gloria’s pencil, a Thursday.

s19.slug: FRIDAY · 1:25 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The night after the storm is cold and scoured and moonless, and the Anchor is still on Jack’s hands: bleach, Hobart steam, the fryer. He coasts La Flaca into the Delgado fire lane at twenty-five past one with Ray’s light throwing a small shaking circle ahead of the front wheel, and in it, on the top step under the lobby light, there is Laney.

She’s in a pink T-shirt that says PI LAM LITTLE in Greek letters and then in English, in case, pulled on over a black party dress with sequins at the hem. She’s barefoot. Her flats are lined up beside her like a pair of patient dogs. A pink balloon is tied to her wrist with curling ribbon and rides above her head in no wind at all, and in her lap is a wicker basket of Pi Lam swag: koozies, a monogrammed tumbler, a picture frame spelling LITTLE in glitter, a wooden paddle. She has had white wine, and her note. She takes the little silver pillbox with DRP on the lid out of the pocket of the party dress (“It has *pockets*, Jack, this dress has *pockets*”), shakes it once like a maraca, and puts it back.
“It was *Big/Little*,” she says, before he’s off the bike. “You have to hear all of it. It’s the law.”

He hears all of it. Clues in her mailbox all week: a Ziploc of Red Hots, a tiny Texas flag, a cassette single of “Kiss Me” because her big was apparently *very* specific. Tonight the scavenger hunt, up and down Seacliff in a blindfold with a sister on each elbow, the porch, a living room full of candles nobody had a permit for, and when the blindfold came off it was Sloane Kittredge holding the paddle. Laney holds it up for him. LANEY in pink glitter. SLOANE in gold. PI LAM LOVE across the bottom, the M running out of room.
“Sloane. The *rush chair*.” Laney puts a hand to her sternum. “I’m *royalty*. I’m Pi Lam royalty. I’m going to need to be addressed differently.”

A Big gives you the family lore, and Sloane’s goes back to 1992. Her big’s big’s big was thrown out of Cabo. “And the pledges used to walk the Point wall,” Laney says. “At midnight. On the *outside*.” She walks her fingertips along the rim of the basket and lets them lurch. “They don’t anymore. Since.”
“Since what?”
“She didn’t say. She looked at her drink.” Laney’s already digging in the basket. “Anyway there’s a *koozie* —”
Then the balloon dips on its ribbon and bumps her on the head, and she bats it away and says to it, laughing, “Kaylee would’ve lost her *mind* —” and hears it, and stops.

body.text: He has heard the name once before, in August, with Laney asleep on his back by the Lagoon and her cheek against his neck. *Kaylee used to — .* Lena’s hand on her back. It never got finished.

body: Laney looks at the balloon. Then at the street.

“Kaylee Whitmore,” she says, first name and last, like roll call. “We were fifteen. Brownies together. Matching everything — we had matching *retainers*, Jack, on purpose. She drove. She had her permit. That’s a joke, a permit.” She smiles at the joke so it’ll know she got it. “There was a party in Preston Hollow, and she’d been drinking and so had I, and I let her. I was in charge of the radio. Preston Road.” She stops. “There’s a culvert.”
The balloon turns on its ribbon. She holds up the wrist it’s tied to, the left one, and turns it in the lobby light like a bracelet she’s showing off.
“Cast for six weeks. Pink. Everybody in the tenth grade signed it.” Her voice doesn’t change at all. “Everybody signed it, and she was dead.”
A truck goes by out on the Anacapa loop with its high beams on, and lights up the Lagoon, and takes the light away again.
“A month later a doctor wrote me a note. For flying.” She laughs, and the laugh is wet. “I’d never been on a plane.”

She tucks her feet under the party dress. “Lena’s the only one who knows. Lena’s the *only* one.” She looks up, at the lobby glass and the floors above it, at the second floor, where she can’t see anything from here. “And I went in her *pocket*.”

Whatever the reason was, it doesn’t come out. Jack watches her go looking for it and come back without it. She looks at him instead, her mascara run to the jaw, holding on to the paddle with both hands.
“Don’t leave,” Laney says. “I’m not drunk. I mean I am. But don’t.”

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows.

choices.text: Sit down beside her and stay.
choices.key: On the Delgado steps at one in the morning, Laney told you about Kaylee.
response: He leans La Flaca on the rail and sits down on the cold step beside her. She puts her head on his shoulder like it’s a place she’s been before. The balloon comes down on its ribbon and bumps him in the ear, and she laughs at that, wet, into the sleeve that smells like the Anchor’s dish pit.

choices.text: “Give me the pillbox, Laney. Just till morning.”
choices.key: On the Delgado steps at one in the morning, Laney told you about Kaylee.
response: She takes the pillbox out of the dress pocket and puts it in his palm. It’s warm from being next to her.
“You sound like her,” Laney says.

choices.key: On the Delgado steps at one in the morning, Laney told you about Kaylee.
response: She laughs properly, from the stomach, and gives the sleeping lobby the wave — wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow — and tells him the rest of the paddle story anyway: the glitter, the hot glue, a sophomore who glued her own palm to the M and had to go to Student Health with it. Then she runs out of story, and goes quiet, and the balloon turns over her head.

s19b.slug: FRIDAY · 1:48 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: Laney is quiet now with her knees pulled up under the party dress, the balloon nodding over her head on its ribbon. Somewhere above them, one floor up and around the east side of the building, Lena has had 217 to herself since Monday.

response: Sent. No reply. He closes the phone.

He leaves the phone where it is. Laney finds a koozie at the bottom of the basket that says PI LAM: WE’RE KIND OF A BIG DEAL and laughs at it, loud, the laugh you can hear across a party, loud enough to carry up a stairwell.

s19c.slug: FRIDAY · 1:52 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The push bar on the lobby door goes, and Lena comes out: the oatmeal cardigan over the green sweatshirt, sleep shorts, her hair down. She’s barefoot on the cold concrete.

body.text: Her LG is in her hand, still open, his text still lit on it.
body.else: “I heard you laugh,” she says to Laney. “Through two doors.”

body: She sits down on Laney’s other side, close, the cardigan against the PI LAM LITTLE shirt.

body.text: Jack holds out the pillbox. Lena takes it without a word, and it goes into her cardigan pocket, and he hears it touch the tin in there, small, metal on metal.

body: Laney keeps her eyes on the paddle. “I’m sorry about your tin.”
“*Cher.* Whose tin do you think that is?” Lena tips her head at Jack, then puts an arm around her, and Laney’s head goes down onto her shoulder, where it fits.
Then, over the top of Laney’s head, to Jack: “I’ve got her, Jack.”

body.text: *Jack.* Not *Mr. Costigan*. He notices that.

body: He gets up. He takes La Flaca around to the rack and chains it, and comes back up past the two of them on the steps, and goes in. Upstairs, in 412, Theo’s screen is lit, a subtitled film, Theo’s back to the room. The Aerobed is still out on the floor, made up tight with somebody’s pageant-grade hospital corners, and empty.

s20.slug: FRIDAY · 12:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE 4TH-FLOOR LOUNGE
body: Friday’s *Tide* is lying on the lounge couch folded open to page three, in the way of a paper that somebody wanted found.

body.title: The Marisol Tide · Friday, Oct. 16 · p. 3
body.text:
CARILLON PLAYED AT DAWN; CAMPUS POLICE ‘LOOKING INTO IT’
By Margot Lindqvist
At approximately 5 a.m. Thursday, an unknown person or persons played ‘When the Saints Go Marching In’ on the Ferrer Tower carillon, which Facilities had closed after Tuesday’s storm. A Facilities spokesperson said the department is ‘not amused.’ Professor Adrian Hale of the Philosophy Department, who said he was awake at the time, called the performance ‘bad, and the first thing that tower has done I’ve enjoyed.’ No suspects have been identified. A Portolá resident, who asked not to be named, said: ‘Honestly? It was kind of epic.’ The tower’s door has been chained.

body: On the whiteboard, under the season’s tally and LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED), there’s a new case in Margot’s block capitals.

body.title: The whiteboard
body.text:
FERRER TOWER · THU 5:00 A.M. · “WHEN THE SAINTS GO MARCHING IN”
SUSPECTS:
1. A CATHOLIC
2. A DIFFERENT CATHOLIC
3. THE HOLY GHOST

body: The third suspect is in pink marker, in bubble letters, with a star after it. Laney has been back in 217 since two this morning.

Margot is at the lounge table with her laptop, typing, the Moleskine closed beside it. She doesn’t look up. “Somebody on this campus,” she says, “has confused a football franchise with a liturgical season and a carillon with a megaphone. I’m not naming anyone. I’m describing a symptom.” Type, type. The Moleskine stays shut by her elbow, and her hands stay on the keys.

body.text: “The police log says an officer observed two individuals fleeing toward the library,” she adds, to the screen. “One of them was laughing.”

body: Lena goes past the lounge door with an empty laundry basket on her hip, headed down the hall toward 412, and thirty seconds later goes back the other way with the basket full of Laney: a hair dryer, a curling iron, two bottles of concealer, a pink BlackBerry charger, one Tory Burch flat. She goes by at the same speed both ways.

journal.title: The whiteboard
journal.text: Margot’s, by annexation: USEFUL IDIOTS FOR CHRISTIAN NATIONALISM, COSTIGAN | BROUSSARD. Sully’s made the board: liturgical football, idolatry, my outfit. Margot wasn’t even there when I read it. She didn’t need to be. Now the chastity talk is up there too: both of us, voluntarily. Kenzie Rourke got her own line. Margot thinks she might not be an idiot. Category pending. C 6, B 5. The morning after the wake, under the total: TUESDAY — NO SCORE. (BEREAVEMENT.) October 9th, top of the board: LEIF ERIKSON DAY (OBSERVED). Columbus: see attached. Then: FERRER TOWER · THU 5:00 A.M. · “WHEN THE SAINTS GO MARCHING IN.” Suspects: a Catholic; a different Catholic. Laney added the Holy Ghost. Margot wrote it up for the Tide and didn’t name anybody.

response: “Baptists would have put it in the bulletin,” Margot says. She hits return.
Margot types for a minute in the silence he’s left her. “Hale told the *Tide* it was played badly,” she says. “Hale has never played anything.” She still hasn’t looked up.

He uncaps the black marker and adds it under the Holy Ghost. Margot gets up, crosses the lounge, and erases it with the side of her fist. “Priya,” she says, “would have laminated it.” She sits back down. It’s the closest she has come all semester to smiling at him, and she conducts it entirely with her eyebrows.

s21.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · MISSION STREET, BECCA’S RANGER OUTSIDE THE RIALTO
body: The Rialto on Mission was a single screen in 1934 and got cut into four in 1987, and the marquee hasn’t been touched since. Tonight it says W ERE THE WILD THI GS ARE, two teeth out, and under that PARANORMAL ACTIVITY, with a line around the corner past the dying Blockbuster. Becca bought their tickets Tuesday, by phone, during the storm. “I’m the one who plans the thing,” she said.

She cried twice in theater three, once when the boy’s mother wouldn’t look up from her work and once at the end, in the boat, and both times she turned to him in the dark to make sure he saw she didn’t know why. Now she sits behind the Ranger’s wheel in the lot with the heater going and her hands on the wheel of a parked truck. St. Isidore rides the visor. The radio is low on KSLY, and she knows every word of the song and doesn’t sing one.

body: “Why is everybody so *sad*?” she says. She read the book to her brothers a hundred times — “a hundred and fifty; Eli made me do the voices, and the voices have to *roar*” — and her favorite line is the last one. She says it now with her chin on the top of the wheel, slowly, savoring it. “*And it was still hot.*”

Then she sits up. “Okay. I have to show you something and you have to be normal about it.” From under the clipboard on the bench seat she takes an envelope, and from the envelope a single sheet of letterhead Jack has known all his life. His mother types on it eight hours a day.

body.title: WE SHOULD MATCH!!
body.text:
1. St. Isidore & St. Maria (farmers!! married!! the only married couple who are both saints)
2. Max & a Wild Thing (I have ears from 4-H)
3. (crossed out) a cowboy & a cow
4. ask Jack

body: He reads it like a problem set. He checks her premises. “Joachim and Anne,” he says.
“Oh!” She looks at the page, betrayed by it. “They’re *older*.”

He asks a clarifying question about the ears. They’re lamb ears, from a 4-H skit about wool, but in low light they could be anything; she demonstrates, hands up on either side of her head. He says they’re good ears. He sits with the list on his knee and can’t pick between a farmer and a Wild Thing, and she waits while he doesn’t, and the song on the radio gets to the part about being fifteen.
“You look at me like I’m homework,” Becca says.

If she’s hurt, it doesn’t get as far as her voice. She says it the way she reads the salinity off the refractometer: what’s there is what’s there. “It’s okay. I know you do. You’re always somewhere else a little.” She takes the clipboard back off his knee. “I don’t mind homework. I’m good at homework.”

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait.

body: His father answers on the second ring, which means he was sitting next to the phone. “Purdue,” Frank says.
“I know.”

“Thirteen-point favorite.” That is the call. There’s a silence on the line with no radio in it, and in the silence Jack can see the garage on Glenwood Avenue, the space heater, the Stroh’s fridge, the radio on the workbench switched off, which it never is. Then his father says, “Here’s your mother,” and is gone.
Ma is brisk, a woman with a pot on. How was the test. Is he sleeping. Then a click on the line, the upstairs extension, and somebody breathing into it carefully, holding it like a seashell.
“Danny?” Nonna says.
The stairwell is very quiet. “No, Nonna. È Giacomino.”
A pause, long enough for the line to hiss in it. Then, warm, unbothered, entirely herself: “Giacomino. Sì. Lo so.” And sharp as a tack, about the one thing: “E la ragazza del granchio?”

body: The light goes gold and long across the Commons at six, and Jack crosses it toward the 6:10 bus and his Saturday shift. The Ferrer Tower stands in the last of the sun with its concrete gone the color of a peach. The caution tape is gone. There’s a new padlock on the steel door, bright brass, and a new Facilities sign zip-tied to the handle, laminated, AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY, in the font of a department that is not amused.

Up in the open chamber the chimes start on their own, on the hour, the way they have since 1966, and the flat bell comes in right where it always does in the phrase, a little low and a little sorry. Then the first of six.

Lena is on the Brick’s front steps with *The Habit of Being* on her knees and a yellow highlighter behind her ear. Her hair is up with a pencil through it. She’s in a sundress for the first warm day in a week, blue with small white flowers, and Keds. On the flat note her head comes up toward the tower; then she finds him, across the grass.

response: He lifts his hand. She holds up five fingers, spread, and over the bell she mouths it: *Tomorrow.*

He holds up five, spread, before she can. She’s offended — a full second of real outrage on the library steps, that he got there first — and then she holds up five right back at him, and mouths it over the bell: *Tomorrow.*

He’s already turned toward the bus stop. He sees it in the bus shelter’s glass instead, small and backward: a girl on the library steps in a blue dress, one hand up, five fingers, and her mouth making the word. *Tomorrow.*

body: The sixth stroke goes out over the Commons and the Lagoon and the roofs of Anacapa and hangs over the water until it isn’t there. The 11 is already idling at the curb on the loop road, nine minutes early, with its doors folded open. Jack gets on and shows his ID and takes a seat on the side facing campus.

As the bus pulls out, the sun is all the way down on the lawn but not yet off the top of the tower. For a minute more it holds there, on the open chamber and the bells hanging dark inside it, one of them flat, all of them gold.
